BCG and the Global Marketing and Media Alliance surveyed roughly 60 chief marketing officers in 2026 and found that AI in marketing has moved beyond experiments. The priority is now enterprise growth—but capturing it requires redesigned workflows, talent models, and agency partnerships.

AI investment is shifting from efficiency to enterprise valueCross-functional, at-scale initiatives now represent more than 21% of AI activity, as leaders connect data and decisions across silos rather than automate isolated marketing tasks.

A clear AI ambition is becoming a practical funding strategyCMOs with mature AI visions are more likely to report adequate funding—62% versus many less-clear peers seeking more—because their plans make the enterprise case for investment.

Technology is absorbing execution work, while human marketers move upstreamAgentic AI—systems that can execute multistep tasks—is expected to rise from 7% to 27% of marketing teams, pushing people toward strategy, judgment, creative direction, and relationship management.

Agencies must shift from capacity suppliers to outcome partnersAgency accountability is expected to fall by 9%–13% across creative and media work. CMOs should therefore build partnerships around shared business outcomes, not time-based staffing models.

A year ago, companies were still debating whether AI would reshape marketing or replace human creativity. Today the commitment to AI is unequivocal, and companies are scaling AI within and across functions to deliver business outcomes, reshaping teams and the way they work. Most importantly, leaders now view AI as an opportunity to deliver enterprise value and growth at the core, not just create efficiencies. Key to that will be human talent moving upstream to be more strategic, creative, and proactive in the business of marketing.To understand AI’s evolving impact on marketing, BCG and the Global Marketing and Media Alliance surveyed about 60 of the world’s most influential chief marketing officers (CMOs) across sectors, from May through July of 2026. We wanted to track how perspectives on AI disruption changed year over year and to explore new questions around financial, operational, and technology issues.Our survey’s major findings include:The C-suite is thinking bigger and moving beyond last year’s focus on AI’s cost-reduction potential, scaling their AI efforts to emphasize enterprise value and innovation.The clearer CMOs are when articulating their AI ambitions, the easier it is to unlock funding for the journey.The accountability for the work of marketing continues to shift dramatically between internal teams, external agencies, and technology, with pressure building for agencies to maximize the business impact of AI.The acceleration of agentic AI will drive major moves in marketing operating models with a particularly profound impact on the talent agenda and client-agency partnership models.The C-Suite Rallies Around Enterprise Value
Compared with last year, the C-suite is more aligned and more optimistic about the value creation opportunities of AI. Beyond the shared belief that AI drives cost efficiency, speed, and productivity, the full C-suite is converging around how this new technology creates potential to innovate products and services, build enterprise value, and drive growth. (See Exhibit 1.)

CMOs, however, remain somewhat isolated in how they think about AI’s promise. They continue to prioritize marketing effectiveness and connecting the customer journey while their C-suite peers articulate more strategic, enterprise-wide priorities. Notably, marketing and technology leaders are finding common ground around personalization as they scale AI across commercial and customer functions.Now that leaders are more aligned, they are starting to think bigger. The share of AI initiatives focused solely on exploration has fallen nine percentage points to 11%, and functional pilots continue to be the single largest category (as they were last year), comprising just over one-third of initiatives. The center of gravity is moving decisively toward scale (growing six percentage points)––more than 21% of AI initiatives are now cross-functional and at-scale.

The center of gravity is moving decisively toward scale (growing six percentage points)––more than 21% of AI initiatives are now cross-functional and at-scale.

The mix of AI initiatives reflects a maturation; companies are moving past using AI for discrete use cases to focus on a more fundamental reimagination of end-to-end workflows and opportunities to connect data and decisions across business silos. The more companies drive toward the ambitious end of the AI spectrum, the more likely they will create enterprise value, deploying dollars for their highest and best use, not simply making functional “assembly lines” more efficient.For marketing specifically, CMOs expect AI to deliver the most tangible business impact in areas of marketing effectiveness and operational efficiency (73% each). But 41% also point to budget reinvestment and new sources of growth. This is evidence that the AI conversation inside marketing parallels the enterprise-wide movement toward value creation.

Shifting CMO Leadership Roles
The AI shift is disrupting the CMO role itself. In our survey, 64% of CMOs say accelerating AI-enabled marketing transformation is a bigger part of their job, and almost half are focused on redesigning the marketing operating model. Overall, the mandate is expanding beyond the marketing function, with 38% driving enterprise-wide transformation.As the job expands, having a clear vision is crucial. CMOs with a mature, well-articulated AI vision are far more likely to have enough funding or more than enough (62%), where marketers who have a less clear vision need a little more or a lot more funding (63%). Put differently, clarity of ambition itself can be a funding strategy. (See Exhibit 2.)

Funding comes from a mix of sources, half from within marketing’s own budgets and half from nonmarketing funds, including enterprise transformation funds, CEO/CFO budgets, and external partners. This underscores that AI in marketing is increasingly treated as an enterprise investment, not simply a functional line item. (See Exhibit 3.)

Substantial Disruptions in End-to-End Workflows
AI is disrupting creative and media workflows differently, but in both cases the shift is substantial. In creative, marketers say adaptation, personalization, and creative testing will most likely be disrupted in the next two to three years. But it’s not a zero-sum game between humans and AI. The research points to new opportunities for humans and AI to collaborate in the creative process, such as in upstream ideation and hero asset creation and more downstream derivative production and asset management. (See Exhibit 4.)

Marketers expect even more fundamental disruption in media workflows than creative workflows, particularly in measurement, optimization, and planning, while the upstream work that requires more human judgment like business planning and media strategy will be less affected.In the cases of both media and creative workflows, executives should place keen attention on specific content types and channels, given the varying degrees of disruption. In general, performance media and key marketing use cases in customer relationship management, such as email, are among the most ripe for AI disruption.

Performance media and key marketing use cases in customer relationship management, such as email, are among the most ripe for AI disruption.

Accountability Is Shifting Among People, Technology, and Partners
The survey shows that the recent trend around accountability is continuing: agencies will take on less of the marketing work while technology will do more over the next few years. Agency accountability for marketing work is anticipated to decline 9% to 13% across creative and media workflows, respectively. At the same time, accountability grew 6% for internal marketing teams, supported by more use of technology (which increased 7% to 6% for creative and media). In both cases, the shifts are anticipated to be more moderate a compared with forecasts a year earlier. (See Exhibit 5.)

Agencies are still a vital part of the mix, but they are under pressure to deliver more aggressively in the context of AI—and marketers have serious doubts about their readiness. Three-quarters of CMOs still say their creative agencies are not prepared to scale AI, though that share has actually improved 11 points year over year. Media agencies have moved the other way: 73% of CMOs now say their media agencies are not AI-ready, up 6 points from last year. Investment in AI technology and upskilling remain the top asks of both partners, followed by different talent, leadership, and structure, and, increasingly, revised commercial models. (See Exhibit 6.)

The survey also showed that AI in marketing will come from a diverse set of sources: 24% from frontier AI and cloud providers, 21% from media owners, 21% from martech/enterprise tech providers, 18% from internally built solutions, 10% from disruptive or point solutions, and 7% from technology offered by independent agencies and disruptors. Continued movement in the mix of providers is very likely.Agentic AI Demands a New Talent and Partnership Model
Disruption from AI will acutely influence the talent agenda. Agentic AI accounts for 7% of the team mix and is expected to nearly quadruple to 27% within two to three years, faster than the pace anticipated a year ago. Agentic AI’s future gains are forecasted to come out of every human category, but not equally. CMOs expect agency talent to fall from 25% to 16%of the mix and freelance from 8% to 5%, while full-timers decline more modestly, from 57% to 48%. The in-house core will remain the biggest part of the talent mix, and developing the capabilities to manage AI will become increasingly crucial. (See Exhibit 7.)

As agentic AI constitutes more of the “team,” CMOs expect the human talent mix to shift upstream and, notably, some work to move in-house. On a five-point scale, CMOs anticipate the mix shifting toward more senior talent (2.6) and slightly in-house over outsourced talent (2.3), while still balancing marketers and technologists, creatives and scientists, and generalists and specialists (3.0 each).Our research bolsters the argument that AI will not simply displace people in specific roles across the marketing value chain. Instead, AI will require a fundamental redesign of workflows and accountability, connecting tasks to create value. AI disruption is a chance for CMOs to redefine internal team structures and build agency relationships as true partnerships, constructed around shared outcomes and value rather than transactional, FTE/time-based models of the past. Wherever the boundary sits between internal and external work, handoffs must be tight enough that signals and value are not lost, bearing in mind that agentic AI will increasingly operate on both sides of that boundary.

The Path Forward
To stay ahead, marketing leaders can take actions that address each of the four shifts we’ve just described that were identified in this year’s survey. Those actions are:Think bigger. The C-suite increasingly measures AI by its contribution to growth, not just efficiency gains. As the function closest to the customer, marketing has opportunities to lead AI-driven growth across the enterprise, building on the C-suite’s growing consensus to tackle bigger problems connecting data and decisions across functions to realize value.Articulate the vision clearly and explicitly. A clear AI vision is both a funding strategy and an execution strategy. CMOs with a well-defined vision are more likely to secure funding from inside and outside the marketing function. It then becomes incumbent on leaders to close the gap on execution––making the vision a reality.Embrace a hybrid workforce. With agentic AI poised to be more than one-quarter of the overall team within a few years, CMOs can help unlock the best combination of human and agentic talent. This includes reimagining new workflows and defining how people and talent can dovetail to create new ways of working. The talent agenda is not solely about upskilling for agentic. It also requires dramatic new approaches to leadership, role definition, structure, partnerships, and organizational incentives.Rewire the operating model with agencies. As accountability continues to change boundaries across internal teams, technology, and agencies, CMOs have an opportunity to redesign the system into a seamless continuum of internal and external capabilities, supported by new agency partnerships and commercial models built for an AI-enabled world.

The next AI wave in marketing will not look like the experiments and pilots of the past. CMOs must execute their vision with a focus on operating in materially new ways, deploying both internal and external capabilities, and seamlessly blending humans and AI to drive growth. There is no singular path, but there is a clear imperative to move quickly.
